howItWorks.flowSubtitle: Here is exactly what happens when you resolve a Pkarr key in this app:
howItWorks.step1Desc: You paste or type a 52-character z-base32 public key. The app strips any prefix like pubky:// or pk: and checks that the key decodes to 32 bytes.
howItWorks.step2Title: The app sends HTTPS requests to relay servers
howItWorks.step2Desc1: The app makes parallel HTTPS GET requests to every enabled relay. By default, it asks:
howItWorks.step2Desc2: Requests are sent at the same time for speed and redundancy. If one relay is down, others can still answer. Each request has a timeout you can change in Settings.
howItWorks.step5Title: The app checks the signature and decodes the DNS packet
howItWorks.step5Desc1: Before anything is shown, the app verifies the Ed25519 signature over the timestamp and the DNS packet with the public key you entered. An answer with a bad signature, or one older than a record already seen, is refused. Then the DNS packet (byte 72 onward) is decoded using the standard DNS wire format. When relays disagree, the newest valid record wins.
howItWorks.step6Desc: The app shows all DNS records in a table. If a web-navigable record is found (HTTPS, SVCB, A, AAAA, or CNAME pointing to a website), a “Visit Website” button gives you the address to open in your browser.
howItWorks.signedDesc: Every DHT record includes a 64-byte Ed25519 signature made by the key owner’s private key. The relay forwards this signature as-is. This app verifies it for every answer, so a record is shown only if the owner of the public key published it and nobody changed it on the way.
howItWorks.redundancyDesc: The app asks multiple relays in parallel. If one relay is down, censored, or malicious, the others can still serve the correct record. You can also add your own relay servers.
howItWorks.faq2Answer: Not a single point: the app uses multiple relays and asks them in parallel. Anyone can run a relay, so the set of available relays is open and decentralized. The relay code is open-source.
howItWorks.faq3Answer: Yes! The Pkarr relay software is open-source. You can run your own instance and add its HTTPS address on the Relays page. This gives you full control over your resolution path.
